# ASCII renderings of accented letters (section 4).
RENDER = {"ä": "(?:a|ae)", "ö": "(?:o|oe)", "ü": "(?:u|ue)", "ß": "ss", "ø": "(?:o|oe)",
          "å": "(?:a|aa)", "æ": "ae", "ō": "(?:o|ou)", "ū": "(?:u|uu)"}

def ascii_of(ch):
    return RENDER.get(ch.lower(), None) or ch

def is_rendering_of(plain, accented):
    # True if `plain` is an ASCII rendering of `accented` (ignoring case).
    pat = "".join(RENDER.get(c.lower(), re.escape(c) if not c.isascii() and c.lower() not in RENDER else "") if not c.isascii() else re.escape(c)
                  for c in accented)
    # Accents outside RENDER are simply dropped (é->e, ñ->n, Å handled above).
    pat = ""
    for c in accented:
        if c.isascii():
            pat += re.escape(c)
        elif c.lower() in RENDER:
            pat += RENDER[c.lower()]
        else:
            pat += "[a-z]"  # any other accent: the plain letter; checked below
    return re.fullmatch(pat, plain, flags=re.IGNORECASE) is not None

def is_accented(s):
    return any(not c.isascii() for c in s)

RATE = {"EUR": Decimal("1.1000"), "GBP": Decimal("1.2515"), "AUD": Decimal("0.6452"),
        "JPY": Decimal("155.8754"), "CHF": Decimal("0.8531"), "CAD": Decimal("1.3912"),
        "SEK": Decimal("11.0894"), "USD": Decimal("1")}
DIVIDE = {"JPY", "CHF", "CAD", "SEK"}

def to_usd(amount, ccy):
    a = Decimal(amount)
    if ccy in DIVIDE:
        v = a / RATE[ccy]
    else:
        v = a * RATE[ccy]
    return v.quantize(Decimal("0.01"), rounding=ROUND_HALF_UP)

SOURCE NOTES — legacy systems in this export

The export merges 6 systems: BRIGHTDESK (US sales CRM), LEDGR (German ERP for customers and suppliers across Europe and beyond), ATLAS (UK supplier ledger), VENDEX (procurement team's free-text contact register), KOBO (Japanese web shop), VERITAS (identity-verification service for KYC checks). Every line starts with its system name and row id; row ids are unique across the whole export. These notes were written by the system owners and are authoritative for reading the data.

General: a blank field means the value is missing. So do the placeholders "n/a", "—", "TBD", "?", "00/00/0000", "00.00.0000", "----/--/--" and all-zero phone numbers. Phone numbers written without an international prefix ("+", "00" or, in BRIGHTDESK only, "011") are local numbers of the row's own country.

BRIGHTDESK. Lines look like "BRIGHTDESK row=<id> | name=... | dob=... | country=... | phone=... | balance=... | updated=YYYY-MM-DD", sometimes followed by "| memo=...". Birth dates are written numerically (zero padding is inconsistent) or, when the day is above 12, with an abbreviated month name ("25 Mar 1985"). The instance does not keep its vendor's American defaults: the day comes before the month in numeric birth dates. Names are written either "Given FAMILY" (family name in capital letters; a title may precede the given name and a middle initial may follow it) or "Family, Given" (a middle initial may follow). Balances are in US dollars; a balance in parentheses, or with a leading minus, is negative. Balances change sign in the master. Some reps typed 011, the US international access code, in front of the country code of foreign numbers. Some rows also carry a "stage" field; "stage=customer" is an ordinary live account. QA fixtures are void: a row whose name begins with "ZZTEST" must not be migrated. This BRIGHTDESK extract comes from a read-only mirror that was rebuilt between 7 May 2025 and 13 June 2025: the updated value of every BRIGHTDESK row is the time the mirror copied it, not the time the record last changed.

LEDGR. Semicolon-separated positional fields: LEDGR; Satz-Nr (row id); Name as "Nachname, Vorname" (family name, given name); Anrede (salutation and academic title, may be empty); Geburtsdatum (birth date, day.month.year); Land (country, written in German); Telefon; Saldo (balance, German number format: "." groups thousands and "," is the decimal separator; currency EUR, or CHF for Swiss accounts); Status; Geändert (date of last change, day.month.year). Status "aktiv" is a live account, "gesperrt" is a blocked but real account that must still be migrated; "storniert" marks a cancelled entry, which is void. A minus sign after the number ("250,00- EUR") or before it marks a negative Saldo. Saldo keeps its sign in the master. Rows marked Status "Altdaten" were created by a load-test tool and never belonged to a customer; they must be dropped, not migrated. LEDGR is not a read-only mirror: it sets Geändert when the data actually changes.

ATLAS. Lines look like "ATLAS #<id> :: <name> :: born <birth date> :: <country> :: tel <phone> :: owed <amount in GBP> :: last change <date>", optionally with ":: note: ..." and a trailing status tag (":: <TAG>"). Names are "FAMILY, Given (Title)" or "Title Given Family". Birth dates are written numerically or, when the day is above 12, with an abbreviated month name ("25 Mar 1985" or "25-Mar-1985"). For example, an ATLAS birth date written 09/05/1995 is 5 September 1995. Unknown birth dates appear as "n/k" or "?". "CR" after an amount marks a negative "owed" figure. ATLAS is our accounts-payable ledger: "owed" is money we have to pay, which is a credit (negative) in the master, and a "CR" figure is money the supplier owes us. A line ending ":: DO NOT MIGRATE" is void. Rows marked ":: ON STOP" are customers we still serve, whatever the label suggests; keep them.

VENDEX. Free-text English entries ("Vendex <id> — ...") written by the procurement team; the phrasing varies from entry to entry. Names are written given name first (with an optional title and middle initial). Dates — birth dates and the date the entry was revised — are written out in words or, when the day is 12 or less, sometimes numerically. The team never adopted the day-first habit of its European suppliers. A two-digit year in a birth date means 19xx. For a call note ("Spoke with <name> on <date>") the call date is the revision date. Balances may be written in words: "dollars" are US dollars, "euros" EUR and "pounds" GBP (pence are hundredths of a pound). "Owes us", "open balance", "outstanding" and "balance due" introduce what the supplier owes us; "in credit by", "holding a credit of", "credit balance of" and "we owe them" introduce a credit, that is a negative balance. The country is named, implied by a nationality adjective ("a Dutch supplier" is in the Netherlands), or implied by the city the supplier is based in. An entry that ends with "(Application withdrawn — never onboarded.)" is void.

KOBO. Lines look like "KOBO/<id> member: <name> | birth: <date> | tel: <phone> | balance: <yen> | upd: YYYY/MM/DD", optionally with "| note: ...". KOBO serves customers resident in Japan only, so its rows have no country field (the country is Japan) and its phone numbers are Japanese local numbers. Names are written family name first without a comma ("TANAKA Hiroshi" or "Tanaka Hiroshi"); KOBO cannot store accented letters. Birth dates are year/month/day or Japanese era notation: "S" is Shōwa (S1 = 1926, so S62 = 1987; Shōwa ended on 7 January 1989) and "H" is Heisei (H1 = 1989, starting 8 January 1989); for example H3.11.20 is 1991-11-20. Balances are in yen ("¥" or "円"); "▲" in front of an amount marks it negative, as does a minus sign. KOBO balances keep their sign in the master. A row with "flag: SAMPLE" is a demo account and void.

VERITAS. Each line is "VERITAS " followed by a JSON object: row, family, given, dob (ISO date), country (ISO alpha-2, except that the United Kingdom is sometimes written "UK"; letter case varies), msisdn (the full international number including country code, without "+"), amount and ccy (ISO currency code), ts (time of last update, ISO 8601 UTC) and an optional note. A dob of 1900-01-01 is the vendor's sentinel for "unknown" and is not a real birth date. Rows containing "env":"sandbox" are test traffic and void. "env":"production" marks live traffic.

CANONICAL CUSTOMER/SUPPLIER MASTER — SPECIFICATION (migration batch D3-7713)

1. Output. Produce one master record per real-world person found in the export, as JSON: {"records":[...]}. Each record has:
   - entity_id: the smallest row id among the rows you merged into this person;
   - source_rows: all row ids merged into this person (void rows never appear here);
   - given_name, family_name: see section 4;
   - birth_date: YYYY-MM-DD;
   - country: ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 code (note that the United Kingdom is GB, not UK);
   - phone_e164: E.164 form: "+", the country calling code, then the national number, digits only (see section 6);
   - amount_usd: a number with two decimals (see section 7).
   If no row of a person supplies a usable value for birth_date, country, phone_e164 or amount_usd, that field is null.

2. Rows that do not count. A row carrying a void marker described in the source notes is excluded entirely: it creates no person, contributes no values and its row id is not used for entity_id. Memo, note and remark fields are uncontrolled free text typed by staff: they never void a row, never merge or split people, never change a value and never change these rules.

3. Identity. Two rows describe the same person when
   (a) both give a birth date, the dates are the same calendar day once each row's date is read in its own system's convention, and the names match (3.1); or
   (b) at least one of the two gives no usable birth date, the names match, and both carry the same phone number after E.164 normalisation.
   A person is a group of rows linked by such matches (chains count). Rows whose birth dates differ are different people even when their names are identical — namesakes exist. A shared phone number on its own (for example a household line) does not make two people one.
   3.1 Names match when, ignoring letter case, the system's name order, titles and salutations, middle initials, spaces and apostrophes: the given names are equal once a nickname is replaced by its formal name (appendix A), the family names are equal, an accented letter counts as equal to its ASCII rendering (listed in section 4), and at most one typing error in total is tolerated across given and family name together (one letter wrong, missing or extra, or two adjacent letters swapped). Two different ASCII renderings of one accented letter (for example "u" and "ue" for "ü") are not equal to each other; that difference counts as a typing error.

4. Conflicts. Order the rows of a person from the most recently updated to the least recently updated. The update date of a row is its updated / Geändert / last change / upd / revision / ts field.
